1

The four questions, and the order to do them

Standing setup for every problem. Good $y$ is the numeraire: $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. Totals: $X = e_{x1}+e_{x2}$, $Y = e_{y1}+e_{y2}$. Person 2 always gets what is left: $x_2 = X - x_1$, $y_2 = Y - y_1$. A person's wealth is the value of their endowment, $W_i = p\,e_{xi} + e_{yi}$, and their budget is $p\,x_i + y_i = W_i$.

Blueprint A

Contract curve (Pareto optimal set). Where do mutually beneficial trades run out? Every allocation where nobody can be made better off without hurting the other.

Blueprint B

Core. Which of those would both people actually accept, starting from $E$? The piece of the contract curve where neither person is worse off than at their endowment.

Blueprint C

Walrasian (competitive) equilibrium. What price $p$ clears both markets when everyone buys their favorite affordable bundle? One price, one allocation. It always lands in the core.

Blueprint D

Lump-sum taxes & transfers. How much wealth do I move so the market lands on the planner's target? Second welfare theorem in action.

Order of operations: A → B → C → D. Even when the homework lists the core as part (a), do the contract curve first — the core is a piece of it, the CE is checked against it, and the tax problem needs a price.

2

Step zero: recognize the utility function

Everything downstream depends on which two types are in the box. Compute $MRS = \dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y}$ for each person and read off the type.

TypeLooks like$MRS = MU_x / MU_y$What it buys you
Cobb–Douglas$x^{a}y^{b}$$\dfrac{a}{b}\cdot\dfrac{y}{x}$ Demand shortcut with $W$ = wealth: $x^* = \dfrac{a}{a+b}\cdot\dfrac{W}{p}$,   $y^* = \dfrac{b}{a+b}\cdot W$. Always buys some of both goods.
Quasi-linear$a\ln x + y$  (or $a\ln x + c\,y$)$\dfrac{a}{x}$  (or $\dfrac{a}{c\,x}$) MRS depends only on $x$. Setting $MRS = p$ gives $x^* = a/p$ with no wealth in it. Get $y$ from the budget afterwards.
Linear (perfect substitutes)$ax + by$$\dfrac{a}{b}$  (a constant) Trades at exactly one price. If this person ends up holding both goods, the price must be $p = a/b$ — they pin the price. Any other price sends them to a corner.
Leontief (perfect complements)$\min\{ax,\; by\}$undefined (kink) Never use MRS. Use the kink line $ax = by$, i.e. $y = \dfrac{a}{b}\,x$ — it is their income expansion path. Any extra of one good is worthless to them.

Read the formula, not the label. HW4 Q3 calls $3x_1 + y_1$ "Leontief" — it is linear. Only a $\min\{\cdot\}$ is Leontief.

3

The ten combos, sorted by how you solve them

Four types, two people: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ mixed pairs plus 4 same-type pairs $= 10$ combos. They collapse into four solution methods, and each method has its own tab with a worked example and a try-it-yourself for every combo in it. Click a cell to jump.

Cobb–DouglasQuasi-linearLinearLeontief
Cobb–Douglas CD + CD1 · smooth + smooth CD + QL1 · smooth + smooth CD + Linear2 · linear pins $p$ CD + Leontief3 · kink line
Quasi-linear same as above QL + QL1 · smooth + smooth QL + Linear2 · linear pins $p$ QL + Leontief3 · kink line
Linear same as abovesame as above Linear + Linear4 · corners Linear + Leontief3 · kink line
Leontief same as abovesame as abovesame as above Leontief + Leontief3 · kink line
Method 1 · Smooth + Smooth

Both have a usable MRS and nobody pins the price. Tangency for the contract curve; add the two $x$-demands to find $p$.

Method 2 · Linear pins the price

A linear person sets $p$ = their MRS before you do anything. Solve the other person; the linear one takes the leftovers.

Method 3 · Leontief kink line

Contract curve = the Leontief person's kink line. Their demand is kink line + budget, two equations.

Method 4 · Linear + Linear

No tangency anywhere. Compare the two constants, send the $x$-lover to a corner, and get $p$ from the budget line through $E$ and that corner.

4

Blueprint A — Contract curve

A

Contract curve (Pareto optimal set)

"Solve for the set of Pareto optimal allocations"
  • 0Write everything in person 1's coordinates: $x_2 = X - x_1$, $y_2 = Y - y_1$.
  • 1Pick the rule for your method (grid below) and write the one equation it gives you.
  • 2Solve it into a shape in $(x_1, y_1)$: a vertical line, a ray, a curve, or two edges. Draw it starting from person 1's origin (bottom-left).
  • 3Edge rule. If your line hits the top or bottom of the box before reaching person 2's corner, the contract curve continues along that edge to the corner.
1 · Smooth + Smooth

Set $MRS_1 = MRS_2$, substitute the totals, solve.

QL–QL → vertical line $x_1 = \bar x$.   CD–QL → a curve like $y_1 = \dfrac{a\,x_1}{X - x_1}$.   CD–CD → a curve from corner to corner.

2 · Linear + Smooth

Set $MRS_{\text{smooth}} = $ the linear person's constant.

Linear–QL → vertical line.   Linear–CD → a ray $y = k\,x$ out of the CD person's origin, then along the edge once it hits.

3 · Leontief + anything

Contract curve = the Leontief person's kink line $ax = by$, drawn from their own origin. No MRS.

If person 2 is the Leontief one, convert: $a(X - x_1) = b(Y - y_1)$. Why it works: off the kink they hold a surplus of one good that gives them zero utility — hand it over and nobody loses.

4 · Linear + Linear

Compare the two constants. The person with the bigger MRS (values $x$ more) gets all the $x$ before anyone gets any $y$.

Two edges (an L). Person 1 is the $x$-lover → bottom edge, then right edge. Person 2 is → left edge, then top edge.

Why the edges count. On an edge, one person has zero of a good. The trade that would help has to be paid for with that good, so it can't happen — no mutually beneficial trade exists, so the point is Pareto optimal. On an exam: draw the edge piece and say that in one sentence.

Running example (used under A, B, C and D): $U_1 = x_1y_1$,   $U_2 = 3\ln x_2 + y_2$,   $e_1 = (2,4)$,   $e_2 = (4,2)$, so $X = Y = 6$. CD + QL → method 1.

0

$MRS_1 = \dfrac{y_1}{x_1}$,   $MRS_2 = \dfrac{3}{x_2} = \dfrac{3}{6 - x_1}$.

1

$$\frac{y_1}{x_1} = \frac{3}{6 - x_1}$$

2

$$y_1 = \frac{3x_1}{6 - x_1}$$ A curve out of person 1's origin that steepens as $x_1$ grows.

3

Edge rule: it reaches the top ($y_1 = 6$) when $3x_1 = 36 - 6x_1$, i.e. $x_1 = 4$. From $(4,6)$ the contract curve runs along the top edge to $(6,6)$.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = \frac{3x_1}{6 - x_1}\ (0 \le x_1 \le 4),\ \text{then the top edge to } (6,6)\;}$$

Blueprint B — Core

B

Core

"Show which allocations are in the core"
  • 1Have the contract curve (Blueprint A).
  • 2Utility at the endowment, one number each: $\bar U_1 = U_1(e_1)$, $\bar U_2 = U_2(e_2)$.
  • 3Plug the contract-curve equation into each utility and require $U_1 \ge \bar U_1$ and $U_2 \ge \bar U_2$. Each inequality gives one endpoint of the core.
  • 4Draw: the two indifference curves through $E$ make a lens. The core is the piece of the contract curve inside the lens. Shade it.
Every diagram on this sheet uses this key.
  • Green curve — person 1's indifference curve through $E$.
  • Copper curve — person 2's indifference curve through $E$ (drawn from the top-right origin).
  • Shaded lens — both at least as well off as at $E$.
  • Dark green line — contract curve.
  • Thick gold — the core: contract curve ∩ lens.
  • Dashed line — budget line through $E$, slope $-p$. The star is the CE. A dotted green line is the budget after taxes, through the target.

Check: the CE from Blueprint C must land inside the core. When exact endpoints need a calculator (logs, cubics), write the two inequalities, shade the lens, and move on — that is what the drawing question is testing.

1

Contract curve from A: $y_1 = \dfrac{3x_1}{6 - x_1}$.

2

$\bar U_1 = 2\cdot 4 = 8$,   $\bar U_2 = 3\ln 4 + 2 \approx 6.16$.

3

Person 1 on the curve: $x_1\cdot\dfrac{3x_1}{6 - x_1} \ge 8 \;\Rightarrow\; 3x_1^2 \ge 48 - 8x_1 \;\Rightarrow\; 3x_1^2 + 8x_1 - 48 \ge 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 \ge \dfrac{-8 + \sqrt{640}}{6} \approx 2.88$.

Person 2 on the curve: $3\ln(6 - x_1) + \left(6 - \dfrac{3x_1}{6 - x_1}\right) \ge 3\ln 4 + 2$. No closed form; numerically $x_1 \le 3.05$.

4

Draw both indifference curves through $E = (2,4)$, shade the lens, mark the piece of the curve with $2.88 \lesssim x_1 \lesssim 3.05$. It is short — $E$ is already close to efficient.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: the piece of } y_1 = \tfrac{3x_1}{6 - x_1} \text{ with } 2.88 \lesssim x_1 \lesssim 3.05\;}$$

6

Blueprint C — Walrasian competitive equilibrium

C

Walrasian equilibrium ($p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$)

"Solve for the CE price ratio and allocation"
  • 0Who pins the price? Look at the grid below before you compute anything.
  • 1Each person: $MRS_i = p$ → write $x_i$ as "stuff with $p$."  QL: $x_i = a_i/p$.  CD: $x_i = \dfrac{a}{a+b}\cdot\dfrac{p\,e_{xi}+e_{yi}}{p}$.  Leontief: kink line + budget → $x_i = \dfrac{W_i}{p + a/b}$.
  • 2Market clearing for $x$: $x_1(p) + x_2(p) = X$. Solve for $p$. (The $y$ market clears automatically — Walras' law.)
  • 3Plug $p$ back in to get $x_1, x_2$.
  • 4Get each $y_i$ from the full budget: $p\,x_i + y_i = \underbrace{p\,e_{xi} + e_{yi}}_{\text{value of endowment}}$.
  • 5Checks: $y_1 + y_2 = Y$; the allocation sits on the contract curve; it sits inside the core; a linear person holds $\ge 0$ of both goods.
1 · Nobody linear

Do steps 1–2: add up the $x$-demands and solve for $p$.

QL–QL: $\dfrac{a_1}{p} + \dfrac{a_2}{p} = X$.   CD or mixed: the demands carry $p$ inside the wealth term — clear fractions and solve.

2 · One linear person

$p = $ their constant MRS, immediately. Do step 1 for the other person only; the linear person gets the leftovers.

Confirm the leftovers are non-negative — that is what justifies $p = $ MRS.

3 · Leontief in the box

Kink line $y = \frac{a}{b}x$ plus budget $p\,x + y = W$ give $x = \dfrac{W}{p + a/b}$. With a CD or QL partner, adding demands gives a quadratic in $p$: factor it and drop the negative root.

4 · Linear + Linear

The CE is the corner from Blueprint A. Get $p$ from person 1's budget line, which must pass through $E$ and the corner: $p\,x_1^{\text{corner}} + y_1^{\text{corner}} = p\,e_{x1} + e_{y1}$.

0

No linear person → add demands.

1

Person 1 (CD, shares $\tfrac12,\tfrac12$): $W_1 = 2p + 4$, so $x_1 = \tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2p + 4}{p} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{p}$.   Person 2 (QL): $x_2 = \dfrac{3}{p}$.

2

$$1 + \frac2p + \frac3p = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac5p = 5 \;\Rightarrow\; p = 1$$

3

$x_1 = 3$,   $x_2 = 3$.

4

$y_1$: $1\cdot 3 + y_1 = 1\cdot 2 + 4 = 6 \Rightarrow y_1 = 3$.   $y_2$: $3 + y_2 = 4 + 2 = 6 \Rightarrow y_2 = 3$.

5

$y_1 + y_2 = 6$ ✓. On the curve: $\dfrac{3\cdot 3}{6 - 3} = 3 = y_1$ ✓. Inside the core ($2.88 \le 3 \le 3.05$) ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 1,\qquad (x_1,y_1) = (3,3),\qquad (x_2,y_2) = (3,3)\;}$$

7

Blueprint D — Lump-sum taxes & transfers

D

Taxes & transfers $(T_1, T_2)$ to reach a target

"Compute the lump-sum taxes and transfers that make the target a CE"
  • 0Supporting price. The target must sit on the contract curve. $p$ = MRS evaluated at the target (use whichever person has an MRS). With a linear person in the box that is just their constant — same $p$ as part (b). Without one, recompute: it usually changes.
  • 1Before: value of each endowment at that $p$: $W_i = p\,e_{xi} + e_{yi}$.
  • 2After: value of each target bundle at that $p$: $V_i = p\,x_i^{T} + y_i^{T}$.
  • 3Difference: $T_i = V_i - W_i$ (after minus before). $T_i \lt 0$ is a tax, $T_i \gt 0$ is a transfer, in units of $y$. Check $T_1 + T_2 = 0$ — the planner only moves wealth, never creates it.
  • 4Write the with-tax budget $p\,x_i + y_i = W_i + T_i$ and confirm that person's demand at wealth $W_i + T_i$ is exactly the target (QL: $x = a/p$; CD: the formula; Leontief: kink + budget; linear: any point on the line).

$$T_i \;=\; \underbrace{\big(p\,x_i^{T} + y_i^{T}\big)}_{\text{value of target}} \;-\; \underbrace{\big(p\,e_{xi} + e_{yi}\big)}_{\text{value of endowment}}$$

Planner's target: $\{(2,\,\tfrac32),\ (4,\,\tfrac92)\}$.

0

On the curve? $\dfrac{3\cdot 2}{6 - 2} = \tfrac32$ ✓. Supporting price: $p = MRS_1 = \dfrac{y_1}{x_1} = \dfrac{3/2}{2} = \dfrac34$ (and $MRS_2 = \dfrac{3}{4}$ ✓). Not the $p = 1$ from step C.

1

Before: $W_1 = \tfrac34(2) + 4 = \tfrac{11}{2}$,   $W_2 = \tfrac34(4) + 2 = 5$.

2

After: $V_1 = \tfrac34(2) + \tfrac32 = 3$,   $V_2 = \tfrac34(4) + \tfrac92 = \tfrac{15}{2}$.

3

Difference: $T_1 = 3 - \tfrac{11}{2} = -\tfrac52$ (tax),   $T_2 = \tfrac{15}{2} - 5 = +\tfrac52$ (transfer). Sum $= 0$ ✓.

4

Verify: person 1 at wealth $3$, $p = \tfrac34$: $x_1 = \tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{3}{3/4} = 2$, $y_1 = \tfrac12\cdot 3 = \tfrac32$ ✓. Person 2: $x_2 = \dfrac{3}{3/4} = 4$, $y_2 = \tfrac{15}{2} - 3 = \tfrac92$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p = \tfrac34,\qquad (T_1, T_2) = \left(-\tfrac52,\; +\tfrac52\right)\;}$$

The running example, all four steps in one picture: contract curve, lens and core, CE on the dashed budget, and the target on the flatter dotted budget ($p = \tfrac34$).
8

Sixty-second sanity checks

  • Did I compute both MRS's and name both types before touching anything else?
  • Does the contract curve start at person 1's origin and end at person 2's (possibly along an edge)?
  • Is the core a sub-piece of the contract curve, inside the lens?
  • Does $x_1 + x_2 = X$ and $y_1 + y_2 = Y$ at the CE?
  • Is the CE on the contract curve and inside the core?
  • If someone is linear: is $p$ equal to their MRS, and do they hold $\ge 0$ of both goods?
  • Taxes: is the target on the contract curve, did I use the price at the target, and does $T_1 + T_2 = 0$?
1

Method 1 — Smooth + Smooth (CD + CD, CD + QL, QL + QL)

both people have a usable MRS; nobody pins the price
  • AContract curve: $MRS_1 = MRS_2$, substitute $x_2 = X - x_1$, $y_2 = Y - y_1$, solve for $y_1$ (QL + QL: you get $x_1 = $ const instead). Edge rule where it hits the top or bottom.
  • BCore: plug the curve into $U_1$ and $U_2$, two inequalities, two endpoints.
  • CCE: $x_1(p) + x_2(p) = X$ with QL: $x = a/p$ and CD: $x = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{W}{p}$. Solve for $p$, plug back, $y$'s from budgets.
  • DTaxes: $p$ = MRS at the target. It changes from part (c) unless the target happens to share the CE's MRS (QL + QL: never changes, since $x_1$ is fixed on the vertical line).

Method 3 — Leontief kink line (Leontief + Linear / CD / QL / Leontief)

$\min\{ax,\,by\}$ in the box
  • AContract curve: the Leontief person's kink line $ax = by \iff y = \frac{a}{b}x$, from their origin. If person 2 is Leontief, convert: $a(X - x_1) = b(Y - y_1)$. Both Leontief with the same kink line → that line.
  • BCore: on the kink line the Leontief utility is just $ax$ (both pieces of the $\min$ are equal), so their inequality is one line of algebra.
  • CCE: Leontief demand = kink line + budget: $p\,x + \frac{a}{b}x = W \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{W}{p + a/b}$. Linear partner → $p$ known, done. CD/QL partner → add demands → a quadratic in $p$: clear denominators, factor, drop the negative root. Leontief partner with the same kink line → every $p$ clears.
  • DTaxes: $p$ = the partner's MRS at the target (Leontief has none). Linear partner → same $p$ as (c); otherwise recompute.

Leontief + Leontief

worked example · edge case

Low priority, but know the shape of it. Two Leontief people have no tradeoffs at all, so this combo behaves strangely: the only clean version is when both kink lines are the same line, and then every price ratio supports an equilibrium. (With different kink lines the Pareto set can be two lines or a whole band — the course problems avoid that.)

Utility & kinks

$U_1 = \min\{x_1,\; 2y_1\}$ → kink $x_1 = 2y_1$, i.e. $y_1 = \tfrac12 x_1$

$U_2 = \min\{x_2,\; 2y_2\}$ → kink $x_2 = 2y_2$

Endowments & totals

$e_1 = (8,2)$,   $e_2 = (4,4)$

$X = 12$,   $Y = 6$

Leontief + LeontiefContract curve: the common kink linePrice: any $p$ clears the market

(a) Contract curve

1

Person 1's kink line: $y_1 = \tfrac12 x_1$.   Person 2's, converted: $12 - x_1 = 2(6 - y_1) \Rightarrow y_1 = \tfrac12 x_1$. The same line.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = \tfrac12 x_1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 12\;}$$

(b) Core

1

$\bar U_1 = \min\{8, 4\} = 4$,   $\bar U_2 = \min\{4, 8\} = 4$.

2

On the line $U_1 = x_1 \ge 4$ and $U_2 = x_2 = 12 - x_1 \ge 4 \Rightarrow x_1 \le 8$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: from } (4,2) \text{ to } (8,4)\;}$$

(c) Walrasian equilibrium

1

Person 1: $p\,x_1 + \tfrac12 x_1 = 8p + 2 \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{8p + 2}{p + \frac12}$.   Person 2: $x_2 = \dfrac{4p + 4}{p + \frac12}$.

2

$$x_1 + x_2 = \frac{12p + 6}{p + \frac12} = \frac{12\left(p + \frac12\right)}{p + \frac12} = 12 \quad\text{for every } p.$$ The market clears at any price.

3

Each $p$ picks a different point of the core: $p = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow x_1 = 6$, $(6,3)$ and $(6,3)$; $p = 1 \Rightarrow x_1 = \tfrac{20}{3}$; $p \to 0 \Rightarrow x_1 \to 4$; $p \to \infty \Rightarrow x_1 \to 8$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Any } p^* \ge 0 \text{ works; the set of CE allocations is the whole core.}\;}$$

Why: neither person has a tradeoff to make — both just want to sit on the diagonal — and a budget line of any slope through $E$ crosses the diagonal somewhere in the core.

Shown for $p = \tfrac12$. Rotate the budget line around $E$ and the star slides along the gold segment.

Method 4 — Linear + Linear (corners)

two constant MRS's, no tangency anywhere
  • AContract curve: compare the constants. The bigger MRS is the $x$-lover; they get all the $x$ before anyone gets any $y$. Person 1 is the $x$-lover → bottom edge then right edge. Person 2 is → left edge then top edge.
  • BCore: one inequality per person on each edge piece.
  • CCE: the corner where the $x$-lover holds all the $x$. $p$ comes from person 1's budget line through $E$ and that corner: $p\,x_1^{c} + y_1^{c} = p\,e_{x1} + e_{y1}$. Check $p$ sits strictly between the two MRS's (so each person really wants only one good).
  • DTaxes: rarely asked; any $p$ between the two MRS's supports a corner target, and before/after/difference works as usual.
1

Linear + Linear

worked example · HW4 Q3

HW typo  The assignment calls these "Leontief," but $3x_1 + y_1$ and $x_2 + 2y_2$ are linear. It also lists "$e_1$" twice — the second one is $e_2 = (3,4)$.

Utility & MRS

$U_1 = 3x_1 + y_1 \;\Rightarrow\; MRS_1 = 3$

$U_2 = x_2 + 2y_2 \;\Rightarrow\; MRS_2 = \dfrac12$

Endowments & totals

$e_1 = (3,2)$,   $e_2 = (3,4)$

$X = 6$,   $Y = 6$

Linear + LinearContract curve: $3 \gt \tfrac12$ → person 1 is the $x$-lover → bottom + right edgesPrice: budget line through $E$ and the corner $(6,0)$

(b) Contract curve

1

$MRS_1 = 3 \gt \tfrac12 = MRS_2$: person 1 would pay up to 3 units of $y$ per unit of $x$; person 2 asks only $\tfrac12$. Whenever both hold some $x$ and some $y$, there is a trade both like.

2

Pareto optimal allocations give person 1 all the $x$ before any $y$: either $y_1 = 0$ (still filling up on $x$) or $x_1 = 6$ (has all the $x$; $y$ is being split).

$$\boxed{\;\text{bottom edge } \{y_1 = 0,\; 0 \le x_1 \le 6\}\ \cup\ \text{right edge } \{x_1 = 6,\; 0 \le y_1 \le 6\}\;}$$

(a) Core

1

$\bar U_1 = 9 + 2 = 11$,   $\bar U_2 = 3 + 8 = 11$.

2

Bottom edge $(x_1, 0)$: $U_1 = 3x_1 \ge 11 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge \tfrac{11}{3}$; $U_2 = (6 - x_1) + 12 \ge 11$ always ✓.   Right edge $(6, y_1)$: $U_1 = 18 + y_1 \ge 11$ always ✓; $U_2 = 2(6 - y_1) \ge 11 \Rightarrow y_1 \le \tfrac12$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: along the bottom from } (\tfrac{11}{3},0) \text{ to } (6,0), \text{ then up to } (6,\tfrac12)\;}$$

(c) Which price ratio(s) support a CE?

0

The CE is the corner: person 1 at $(6,0)$, person 2 at $(0,6)$.

1

Budget line through $E$ and the corner: $p\cdot 6 + 0 = p\cdot 3 + 2 \Rightarrow 3p = 2 \Rightarrow p = \tfrac23$.

2

Consistency: $\tfrac12 \lt \tfrac23 \lt 3$, so person 1 wants only $x$ and person 2 only $y$ ✓. Person 2's wealth $3(\tfrac23) + 4 = 6 = y_2$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = \tfrac23,\qquad (6,0),\qquad (0,6)\;}$$

Why only one price? Any $p$ strictly between $\tfrac12$ and $3$ sends both to their corners, but person 1 can afford exactly 6 units of $x$ only when $3 + 2/p = 6$, i.e. $p = \tfrac23$. At $p \ge 3$ or $p \le \tfrac12$ someone is indifferent and the markets still don't clear. A range of prices appears only in the second-welfare-theorem version, where a planner moves wealth first.

The lens is the region between the two straight indifference curves; the core is the gold piece of the L inside it; the CE is the corner.

Check $\tfrac13 \lt \tfrac32 \lt 2$ ✓. Person 2's wealth $2(\tfrac32) + 6 = 9 = \tfrac32\cdot 6$: buys exactly the 6 units of $x$ ✓.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Set up the core.

(a) Contract curve
1

$$\frac{2y_1}{x_1} = \frac{16 - y_1}{12 - x_1} \;\Rightarrow\; 2y_1(12 - x_1) = x_1(16 - y_1)$$

2

$24y_1 - 2x_1y_1 = 16x_1 - x_1y_1 \Rightarrow 24y_1 - x_1y_1 = 16x_1 \Rightarrow y_1 = \dfrac{16x_1}{24 - x_1}$.   Check: $x_1 = 12 \Rightarrow y_1 = 16$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = \frac{16x_1}{24 - x_1},\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 12\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
1

$W_1 = 6p + 12 \Rightarrow x_1 = \tfrac23\cdot\dfrac{6p + 12}{p} = 4 + \dfrac8p$.   $W_2 = 6p + 4 \Rightarrow x_2 = \tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{6p+4}{p} = 3 + \dfrac2p$.

2

$$7 + \frac{10}{p} = 12 \;\Rightarrow\; p = 2$$

$x_1 = 8$, $x_2 = 4$;   $y_1 = \tfrac13 W_1 = \tfrac13(24) = 8$,   $y_2 = \tfrac12 W_2 = \tfrac12(16) = 8$.   Sums $12$, $16$ ✓; on the curve: $\dfrac{16\cdot 8}{16} = 8$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 2,\qquad (8,8),\qquad (4,8)\;}$$

$\bar U_1 = 36\cdot 12 = 432$,   $\bar U_2 = 24$. On the curve: $x_1^2\cdot\dfrac{16x_1}{24 - x_1} \ge 432$ and $(12 - x_1)\left(16 - \dfrac{16x_1}{24 - x_1}\right) \ge 24$ → numerically $7.62 \lesssim x_1 \lesssim 8.60$. The CE ($x_1 = 8$) is inside ✓.

$U_1 = x_1 y_1$,   $U_2 = 4\ln x_2 + y_2$,   $e_1 = (6,2)$,   $e_2 = (2,6)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.

(a) Contract curve
1

$$\frac{y_1}{x_1} = \frac{4}{8 - x_1} \;\Rightarrow\; y_1 = \frac{4x_1}{8 - x_1}$$

2

Hits the top ($y_1 = 8$) when $4x_1 = 64 - 8x_1 \Rightarrow x_1 = \tfrac{16}{3}$; then along the top edge to $(8,8)$.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = \frac{4x_1}{8 - x_1}\ (0 \le x_1 \le \tfrac{16}{3}),\ \text{then the top edge}\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
1

$x_1 = \tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{6p + 2}{p} = 3 + \dfrac1p$,   $x_2 = \dfrac4p$.

2

$$3 + \frac1p + \frac4p = 8 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac5p = 5 \;\Rightarrow\; p = 1$$

3

$x_1 = 4$, $x_2 = 4$;   $y_1 = \tfrac12(6 + 2) = 4$,   $y_2 = 8 - 4 = 4$ (check: $4 + 4 = 8 = 2 + 6$ ✓). On the curve: $\dfrac{16}{4} = 4$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 1,\qquad (4,4),\qquad (4,4)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 12$,   $\bar U_2 = 4\ln 2 + 6 \approx 8.77$.   Person 1: $\dfrac{4x_1^2}{8 - x_1} \ge 12 \Rightarrow x_1^2 + 3x_1 - 24 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{105}}{2} \approx 3.62$. Person 2: $4\ln(8 - x_1) + 8 - \dfrac{4x_1}{8 - x_1} \ge 8.77$ → numerically $x_1 \le 4.24$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: } 3.62 \lesssim x_1 \lesssim 4.24 \text{ on the curve}\;}$$

$U_1 = 4\ln x_1 + y_1$,   $U_2 = 2\ln x_2 + y_2$,   $e_1 = (2,4)$,   $e_2 = (4,2)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.   (d) Taxes to reach $\{(4,1),\,(2,5)\}$.

(a) Contract curve
1

$$\frac{4}{x_1} = \frac{2}{x_2} \;\Rightarrow\; x_2 = \frac{x_1}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac32 x_1 = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 = 4$$

$$\boxed{\;x_1 = 4,\ 0 \le y_1 \le 6,\ \text{plus the bottom edge left and the top edge right}\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
1

$x_1 = \dfrac4p$, $x_2 = \dfrac2p$;   $\dfrac6p = 6 \Rightarrow p = 1$.

2

$x_1 = 4$, $x_2 = 2$;   $y_1 = (2 + 4) - 4 = 2$,   $y_2 = (4 + 2) - 2 = 4$. ✓

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 1,\qquad (4,2),\qquad (2,4)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 4\ln 2 + 4$,   $\bar U_2 = 2\ln 4 + 2$. On $x_1 = 4$: $4\ln 4 + y_1 \ge 4\ln 2 + 4 \Rightarrow y_1 \ge 4 - 4\ln 2 \approx 1.23$;   $2\ln 2 + (6 - y_1) \ge 2\ln 4 + 2 \Rightarrow y_1 \le 4 - 2\ln 2 \approx 2.61$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: } x_1 = 4,\ 4 - 4\ln 2 \le y_1 \le 4 - 2\ln 2\;}$$

(d) Taxes & transfers
0

$x_1 = 4$ ✓ on the line; $p = 1$.

1

Before: $W_1 = 6$, $W_2 = 6$.   After: $V_1 = 4 + 1 = 5$, $V_2 = 2 + 5 = 7$.   Difference: $T_1 = -1$, $T_2 = +1$. Verify: person 1 at wealth 5: $x_1 = 4$, $y_1 = 1$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;(T_1, T_2) = (-1,\; +1)\;}$$

$U_1 = x_1^{2}\,y_1$,   $U_2 = x_2 + 2y_2$,   $e_1 = (2,2)$,   $e_2 = (6,6)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.   (d) Taxes to reach $\{(8,2),\,(0,6)\}$.

(a) Contract curve
1

$$\frac{2y_1}{x_1} = \frac12 \;\Rightarrow\; y_1 = \frac{x_1}{4}$$ A ray from person 1's origin; it reaches the right edge at $(8,2)$ before the top.

2

Edge rule: from $(8,2)$ up the right edge to $(8,8)$. (There person 2 has no $x$; he would sell $x$ for $y$ but has none.)

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = \tfrac14 x_1\ (0 \le x_1 \le 8),\ \text{then the right edge } x_1 = 8\ (2 \le y_1 \le 8)\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
0

$p = \tfrac12$.

1

$W_1 = \tfrac12(2) + 2 = 3$.   $x_1 = \tfrac23\cdot\dfrac{3}{1/2} = 4$,   $y_1 = \tfrac13\cdot 3 = 1$.

2

Person 2 gets $(4,7)$; check $\tfrac12(4) + 7 = 9 = 3 + 6$ ✓; both positive ✓; on the ray ($1 = 4/4$) ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = \tfrac12,\qquad (4,1),\qquad (4,7)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 8$,   $\bar U_2 = 6 + 12 = 18$. On the ray: $U_1 = x_1^2\cdot\tfrac{x_1}{4} = \tfrac{x_1^3}{4} \ge 8 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 32^{1/3} \approx 3.17$;   $U_2 = (8 - x_1) + 2(8 - \tfrac{x_1}{4}) = 24 - \tfrac32 x_1 \ge 18 \Rightarrow x_1 \le 4$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: the ray from } (3.17, 0.79) \text{ to } (4,1);\ \text{CE at the linear end}\;}$$

(d) Taxes & transfers
0

$(8,2)$ is where the ray meets the edge: on the contract curve ✓. $p = \tfrac12$.

1

Before: $W_1 = 3$, $W_2 = 9$.   After: $V_1 = \tfrac12(8) + 2 = 6$, $V_2 = 0 + 6 = 6$.   Difference: $T_1 = +3$, $T_2 = -3$. Verify: person 1 at wealth 6: $x_1 = \tfrac23\cdot\tfrac{6}{1/2} = 8$, $y_1 = 2$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;(T_1, T_2) = (+3,\; -3)\;}$$

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.   (d) Taxes to reach $\{(4,1),\,(4,5)\}$.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 8$, $Y = 6$.   $\dfrac{4}{x_1} = 1 \Rightarrow x_1 = 4$.

$$\boxed{\;x_1 = 4,\ 0 \le y_1 \le 6,\ \text{plus the bottom edge left and the top edge right}\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
0

$p = 1$.

1

$x_1 = 4$;   $W_1 = 2 + 4 = 6 \Rightarrow y_1 = 6 - 4 = 2$. Person 2 gets $(4,4)$; check $4 + 4 = 8 = 6 + 2$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 1,\qquad (4,2),\qquad (4,4)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 4\ln 2 + 4$,   $\bar U_2 = 8$. On $x_1 = 4$: $4\ln 4 + y_1 \ge 4\ln 2 + 4 \Rightarrow y_1 \ge 4 - 4\ln 2 \approx 1.23$;   $4 + (6 - y_1) \ge 8 \Rightarrow y_1 \le 2$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: } x_1 = 4,\ 4 - 4\ln 2 \le y_1 \le 2;\ \text{CE at the linear end } (y_1 = 2)\;}$$

(d) Taxes & transfers
1

$p = 1$. Before: $W_1 = 6$, $W_2 = 8$. After: $V_1 = 5$, $V_2 = 9$. Difference: $T_1 = -1$, $T_2 = +1$. Verify: person 1 at wealth 5: $x_1 = 4$, $y_1 = 1$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;(T_1, T_2) = (-1,\; +1)\;}$$

$U_1 = 4x_1 + 2y_1$,   $U_2 = \min\{x_2,\; 2y_2\}$,   $e_1 = (9,4)$,   $e_2 = (3,4)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.   (d) Taxes to reach $\{(10,7),\,(2,1)\}$.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 12$, $Y = 8$. Kink: $x_2 = 2y_2 \Rightarrow 12 - x_1 = 2(8 - y_1) \Rightarrow y_1 = 2 + \dfrac{x_1}{2}$.

2

It runs from $(0,2)$ on the left edge to person 2's corner $(12,8)$. (Below $(0,2)$ person 2 would hold surplus $y$ — not Pareto optimal.)

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = 2 + \tfrac12 x_1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 12\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
0

$p = MRS_1 = 2$.

1

Person 2: $y_2 = \tfrac12 x_2$ and $2x_2 + \tfrac12 x_2 = 2(3) + 4 = 10 \Rightarrow \tfrac52 x_2 = 10 \Rightarrow x_2 = 4,\ y_2 = 2$.

2

Person 1 gets $(8,6)$; check $2(8) + 6 = 22 = 2(9) + 4$ ✓; on the line ($2 + 4 = 6$) ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 2,\qquad (8,6),\qquad (4,2)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 36 + 8 = 44$,   $\bar U_2 = \min\{3, 8\} = 3$. On the line: $U_1 = 4x_1 + 2(2 + \tfrac{x_1}{2}) = 5x_1 + 4 \ge 44 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 8$;   $U_2 = x_2 = 12 - x_1 \ge 3 \Rightarrow x_1 \le 9$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: from } (8,6) \text{ to } (9, 6.5);\ \text{CE at the linear end}\;}$$

(d) Taxes & transfers
1

On the line ($2 + 5 = 7$) ✓; $p = 2$. Before: $W_1 = 22$, $W_2 = 10$. After: $V_1 = 20 + 7 = 27$, $V_2 = 4 + 1 = 5$. Difference: $T_1 = +5$, $T_2 = -5$. Verify: person 2 at wealth 5: $\tfrac52 x_2 = 5 \Rightarrow x_2 = 2$, $y_2 = 1$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;(T_1, T_2) = (+5,\; -5)\;}$$

$U_1 = \min\{3x_1,\; y_1\}$,   $U_2 = x_2 y_2$,   $e_1 = (1,9)$,   $e_2 = (3,3)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 4$, $Y = 12$. Kink line $y_1 = 3x_1$ from $(0,0)$ to $(4,12)$ — corner to corner.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = 3x_1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 4\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
1

Person 1: $p\,x_1 + 3x_1 = p + 9 \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{p + 9}{p + 3}$.   Person 2: $x_2 = \tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{3p + 3}{p} = \dfrac{3(p + 1)}{2p}$.

2

$$\frac{p + 9}{p + 3} + \frac{3(p+1)}{2p} = 4$$ Multiply by $2p(p + 3)$: $\;2p(p + 9) + 3(p + 1)(p + 3) = 8p(p + 3) \Rightarrow 5p^2 + 30p + 9 = 8p^2 + 24p \Rightarrow 3p^2 - 6p - 9 = 0 \Rightarrow p^2 - 2p - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow (p - 3)(p + 1) = 0 \Rightarrow p = 3$.

3

$x_1 = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2$, $y_1 = 6$;   $x_2 = \dfrac{3\cdot 4}{6} = 2$, $y_2 = \tfrac12(9 + 3) = 6$. Sums $4, 12$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 3,\qquad (2,6),\qquad (2,6)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = \min\{3, 9\} = 3$,   $\bar U_2 = 9$. On the kink line: $U_1 = 3x_1 \ge 3 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 1$;   $U_2 = (4 - x_1)(12 - 3x_1) = 3(4 - x_1)^2 \ge 9 \Rightarrow x_1 \le 4 - \sqrt3 \approx 2.27$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: from } (1,3) \text{ to } (4 - \sqrt3,\; 12 - 3\sqrt3);\ \text{CE } (2,6) \text{ inside}\;}$$

$U_1 = \min\{2x_1,\; y_1\}$,   $U_2 = 6\ln x_2 + y_2$,   $e_1 = (4,4)$,   $e_2 = (2,8)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Walrasian equilibrium.   (c) Core.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 6$, $Y = 12$. Kink line $y_1 = 2x_1$ from $(0,0)$ to $(6,12)$.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = 2x_1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 6\;}$$

(b) Walrasian equilibrium
1

Person 1: $p\,x_1 + 2x_1 = 4p + 4 \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{4p + 4}{p + 2}$.   Person 2: $x_2 = \dfrac6p$.

2

$$\frac{4p + 4}{p + 2} + \frac6p = 6$$ Multiply by $p(p + 2)$: $\;4p^2 + 4p + 6p + 12 = 6p^2 + 12p \Rightarrow 2p^2 + 2p - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow p^2 + p - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (p + 3)(p - 2) = 0 \Rightarrow p = 2$.

3

$x_1 = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3$, $y_1 = 6$;   $x_2 = 3$, $y_2 = (4 + 8) - 6 = 6$. Sums $6, 12$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = 2,\qquad (3,6),\qquad (3,6)\;}$$

(c) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = \min\{8, 4\} = 4$,   $\bar U_2 = 6\ln 2 + 8 \approx 12.16$. On the kink line: $U_1 = 2x_1 \ge 4 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 2$;   $U_2 = 6\ln(6 - x_1) + (12 - 2x_1) \ge 12.16$ → numerically $x_1 \le 3.11$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: from } (2,4) \text{ to about } (3.11, 6.21);\ \text{CE } (3,6) \text{ inside}\;}$$

$U_1 = \min\{2x_1,\; y_1\}$,   $U_2 = \min\{2x_2,\; y_2\}$,   $e_1 = (1,6)$,   $e_2 = (4,4)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Core.   (c) Which price ratio(s) support a CE? Give the allocation at $p = 2$.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 5$, $Y = 10$. Person 1: $y_1 = 2x_1$. Person 2: $10 - y_1 = 2(5 - x_1) \Rightarrow y_1 = 2x_1$. Same line.

$$\boxed{\;y_1 = 2x_1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 5\;}$$

(b) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = \min\{2, 6\} = 2$,   $\bar U_2 = \min\{8, 4\} = 4$. On the line: $2x_1 \ge 2 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge 1$;   $2(5 - x_1) \ge 4 \Rightarrow x_1 \le 3$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: from } (1,2) \text{ to } (3,6)\;}$$

(c) Equilibrium prices
1

$x_1 = \dfrac{p + 6}{p + 2}$,   $x_2 = \dfrac{4p + 4}{p + 2}$,   sum $= \dfrac{5p + 10}{p + 2} = 5$ for every $p$.

2

At $p = 2$: $x_1 = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$, $y_1 = 4$; person 2 gets $(3,6)$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Any } p \ge 0;\ \text{at } p = 2:\ (2,4),\ (3,6)\;}$$

$U_1 = 4x_1 + y_1$,   $U_2 = x_2 + y_2$,   $e_1 = (1,5)$,   $e_2 = (3,1)$.

(a) Contract curve.   (b) Core.   (c) Walrasian equilibrium price and allocation.

(a) Contract curve
1

$X = 4$, $Y = 6$. Person 1 values $x$ more ($4 \gt 1$), so Pareto optimal allocations give person 1 all the $x$ before any $y$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{bottom edge } \{y_1 = 0,\ 0 \le x_1 \le 4\}\ \cup\ \text{right edge } \{x_1 = 4,\ 0 \le y_1 \le 6\}\;}$$

(b) Core
1

$\bar U_1 = 9$,   $\bar U_2 = 4$. Bottom $(x_1, 0)$: $4x_1 \ge 9 \Rightarrow x_1 \ge \tfrac94$; $U_2 = (4 - x_1) + 6 \ge 4$ always. Right edge $(4, y_1)$: $U_1 = 16 + y_1 \ge 9$ always; $U_2 = 6 - y_1 \ge 4 \Rightarrow y_1 \le 2$.

$$\boxed{\;\text{Core: along the bottom from } (\tfrac94, 0) \text{ to } (4,0), \text{ then up to } (4,2)\;}$$

(c) Walrasian equilibrium
1

Corner $(4,0)$ for person 1. Budget through $E$ and the corner: $4p = p + 5 \Rightarrow p = \tfrac53$. Check $1 \lt \tfrac53 \lt 4$ ✓. Person 2 gets $(0,6)$; wealth $3(\tfrac53) + 1 = 6$ ✓.

$$\boxed{\;p^* = \tfrac53,\qquad (4,0),\qquad (0,6)\;}$$
